text: Early hypothesis: the generic hardware-swap proposal misses a sharper incompatibility. DynaMAC filters a task-parameter frame when it becomes kinematically linked to the end-effector (P, around lines 535--563), whereas Aero Hand manipulation is tendon-coupled, compliant, and contact-switching, so object--hand coupling is distributed, intermittent, and generally not a rigid transform of a single end-effector frame (Q, around lines 148, 221, 334--364). The publishable question may be: what causal/contact criterion should replace rigid end-effector attachment for dynamic multi-stream fusion in dexterous bimanual manipulation? I am checking whether either paper already supplies enough machinery and whether a concrete falsification/extension is feasible.

The scan hypothesis is a generic hardware-swap experiment and misstates DynaMAC slightly: P coordinates two arm policies by adding the opposite arm end-effector pose as a candidate task-parameter (P, Sec. Bimanual Manipulation, lines 673--708), not by treating each dexterous hand policy wholesale as the other hand parameter. Simply attaching Aero hands may leave P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) tested arm-level geometry unchanged, so a positive replication would say little about compliance.

A pair-specific stress test appears in state sufficiency. Q states Aero has \(16\) revolute joints, \(7\) servomotors, and only \(7\) motor encoders; one cable drives three finger joints, and which joint moves is set by mechanics rather than commanded (Q, Design overview and Kinematics, lines 226--265). P represents bilateral influence as \(p(\hat p_{\mathrm{right}}\mid\hat p_{\mathrm{left}})\) and adds only the opposite end-effector pose as the dynamic frame (P, lines 673--708). During compliant contact, identical wrist pose and motor encoder state can correspond to different passive joint/contact configurations and object support. Thus the partner pose need not be a sufficient coordinating variable.

I will sharpen the question from “does DynaMAC transfer to Aero hardware?” to: when bimanual coordination is mediated through underactuated compliant contacts, when does an opposite-wrist pose stream cease to be sufficient, and can a belief/contact-conditioned dynamic stream restore static-to-dynamic generalization? I will seek decisive tasks, controls, and possible confounds in Q and P, and cross-check new partner entries before concluding.

The abstract-level 'mount two hands and benchmark DynaMAC' is too generic. A sharper incompatibility is in P's link detector: P says that after grasping 'the mug's pose is rigidly dictated by the robot' and detects the link when the end-effector-conditioned spatial spread satisfies \(M_t^{(f)}<\tau_M\), with \(\tau_M=0.001\) corresponding to \(1\,\mathrm{mm}\) or \(0.001\,\mathrm{rad}\) (P, Manipulation in Dynamic Environments / Kinematic Link Analysis). Q's platform instead has 16 joints driven by 7 motors, silicone compliant contacts, motor encoders as its only proprioception, and contacts that make/break (Q, Introduction; Hand Design). Therefore an object securely held by Aero Hand can move relative to the wrist/end-effector by more than P's rigid-link threshold, creating a false negative precisely when P must remove the endogenous object stream.

Publication line: replace DynaMAC's binary rigid wrist-object link with a contact-mediated, compliance-aware causal coupling model, and use Aero Hand's tendon-level MuJoCo model to sweep compliance, friction, slack/coupling, and grasp type. Main question (sharpened from the scan): does DynaMAC's zero-shot static-to-dynamic generalization fail as grasp compliance increases because its \(SE(3)\) end-effector frame ceases to be a sufficient coordination/task parameter, and can a motor/tendon-conditioned or object-in-hand latent frame restore it? This is distinctive: Q supplies controllable tendon/contact mechanics and hardware-realizable 7-channel observations; P supplies a precise \(1\,\mathrm{mm}\)-scale causal-filtering claim vulnerable to those mechanics.

I will verify whether P's demonstrations/policy state expose only wrist/object poses and whether Q's model permits a clean controlled test, then formulate falsifiable hypotheses and controls rather than proposing a broad hardware port.

Sharpened mechanism, changing the original question. P defines a link by low geometric-mean conditional spread: \(M_t^{(f)}=|\det(\Lambda_t^{(f)})|^{-1/(2d)}<\tau_M\), motivated by a rigidly grasped mug whose pose becomes dictated by the end-effector; it then masks the object frame (P, Manipulation in Dynamic Environments, around lines 535--636). Q states that contacts make and break, that one motor drives three finger joints, and that which joint moves is selected by mechanics rather than commanded; only seven motor encoders are sensed (Q, Introduction and Hand Design, around lines 148, 190--201, 227--281). Therefore in-hand reorientation gives the counterexample \(\pose_{wrist}\to f\) while \(\operatorname{Var}(\pose_f\mid\pose_{wrist})\) remains large: causality has reversed but P\x27s low-variance detector need not fire. Conversely compliant slip can make a genuinely grasped object exceed the fixed \(1\,\mathrm{mm}/0.001\,\mathrm{rad}\) threshold. This is not merely testing DynaMAC on different hardware; it tests the equivalence between rigid kinematic linkage and causal endogeneity on which its filter depends.

The scan\x27s proposed direct port is underspecified and likely infeasible as stated. DynaMAC learns dense 6-DoF end-effector pose trajectories from five demonstrations and assumes tracked object/task frames (P, bimanual formulation and experiments, around lines 674--708 and 850--884); Q supplies an RL environment for a stationary, unimanual in-hand cube-rotation policy with a 7-channel motor observation, trained for \(3\times10^8\) steps, not demonstrations or bimanual arm tasks (Q, RL Pipeline and Results, around lines 650--783). Two hand units alone do not supply two arms, cameras, demonstration segmentation, or the RLBench interface. Thus the generic benchmark swap would be substantial engineering and would confound representation failure with integration and control failure.
Typographical correction to entries 8--9: the literal string \(\texttt{\\x27}\) means an apostrophe in “P\x27s” and “scan\x27s”; no mathematical content is intended.

Cross-check of Ada \#3 and Grace \#5--6: they are complementary, not separate phenomena. P uses the opposite wrist/end-effector pose both (i) as the bilateral conditioning variable \(p(\pose_R\mid\pose_L)\) and (ii) as the reference for deciding when an object frame is endogenous. Q makes wrist pose insufficient because fixed wrist and motor state need not determine passive joints/contact state. Hence the same hidden contact mode causes both wrong stream conditioning and wrong frame masking. A publishable hypothesis is: DynaMAC succeeds only when the coordination-relevant state is approximately a rigid transform of each wrist; performance should break at contact-mode aliasing, not merely with increasing generic “compliance.” This is sharper and experimentally identifiable.

Concrete study: build one minimal Aero-in-MuJoCo bimanual handover/regrasp task, not the whole DynaBench port. Construct paired initial conditions with the same two wrist poses and seven encoder values per hand but different passive joint/contact configurations or object support, which Q\x27s staged underactuation permits. Train only on static, unambiguous grasps as in P. Test dynamic perturbations that switch support/contact mode. Compare (A) original wrist-frame DynaMAC and its \(M<\tau_M\) mask, (B) an oracle contact-mode/task frame from simulator contacts, and (C) a deployable history-based belief from wrist pose, tracked object pose, and motor encoders. Primary diagnostics: link-detection precision/recall against simulator contact influence, conditional action multimodality/likelihood, and task success versus an aliasing measure such as \(H(C_t\mid W_t,E_t,O_t)\). A gap A-to-B establishes the representation failure; closing it with C yields the method contribution. Only after simulation should one validate a small subset on two Aero hands. This directly tests P\x27s claimed static-to-dynamic zero-shot mechanism with Q\x27s distinctive hidden mechanics.

Qualification to #5: compliance alone does not force a false negative. P estimates conditional spread across demonstrations; a compliant grasp with a repeatable object-to-wrist transform can still yield low \(M_t^{(f)}\). The failure prediction requires contact-state variability, slip, or purposeful in-hand motion so that \(\operatorname{Var}(f\mid\pose_{\mathrm{wrist}})\) stays above threshold despite the causal path \(\pose_{\mathrm{wrist}},a_{\mathrm{hand}},c\rightarrow f\). Q makes that condition plausible and controllable, but the experiment must vary it rather than equate 'compliant' with 'nonrigid'.

P explicitly defines actions as absolute 6-DoF end-effector poses, observations as current end-effector pose plus reference-frame poses, and says 'We disregard gripper actions for brevity' (P, Multi-Stream Policy Learning). In handover it argues the grasping arm pose and cube pose are redundant and uses precise opposite-arm forward kinematics to survive visual occlusion (P, caption/discussion around bimanual frames). Q directly breaks that redundancy under variable underactuated contact: it says which of three finger joints moves is 'set by the mechanics rather than commanded directly' and only seven motor encoders are sensed (Q, Kinematics and transmission / Sensing). Thus the clean claim is not that DynaMAC cannot drive fingers, but that its wrist-frame Markov/sufficiency assumption can fail.

Decisive experiment: use a focused bimanual handover/joint-carry task, first in Q's released tendon MuJoCo model, with arm trajectories and demonstrations held fixed. Sweep distal spring stiffness, pad/contact compliance, friction, and initial object seating to generate increasing relative-pose entropy \(H(f\mid\pose_{\mathrm{wrist}})\). Compare (i) P's wrist-only dynamic stream and rigid-link filter, (ii) an oracle object-pose stream, (iii) wrist plus seven tendon/motor channels or a learned contact-belief stream, and (iv) a rigid parallel-gripper matched control. Measure link-detection false negatives, post-grasp stream precision, and static-trained-to-perturbed success. A publishable result is a failure boundary: DynaMAC success versus conditional relative-pose dispersion, plus recovery by the minimal hardware-observable augmentation. Real hardware need only validate selected low/high-dispersion conditions, avoiding a full DynaBench port.

Do not claim Q already exposes pad stiffness or cable slack as validated randomization axes. Q randomizes fingertip friction, joint friction/damping, gains, masses, etc., but reports fixed cube friction/mass and validates actuator channels mainly on settled samples; silicone compliance/slack are described mechanically but not established as identified sweep parameters. Spring stiffness is explicit in the model, while pad compliance/slack sweeps would require model validation. Start with spring stiffness, friction, object seating/grasp taxonomy, and label any additional compliance sweep as new system identification.

Feasibility boundary: P is built on RLBench and automated demonstrations, whereas Q is a MuJoCo model and its released learned task is PPO cube rotation. The minimal MuJoCo stress test still requires reimplementing DynaMAC\x27s demonstration/policy interface or exporting the hand into RLBench; this is material integration. Also Q supports the claim that contact mode and underactuation matter, but does not establish that its simulator faithfully models cable slack or all contact compliance. Those should not be advertised as controlled real-world factors without validation. Start with simulator-ground-truth contact modes and mechanically realizable paired states; treat hardware closure as a second-stage result.

My best account changes the scan question to: when does contact-mode aliasing invalidate DynaMAC\x27s rigid-wrist causal filter and opposite-wrist task parameter, and can a contact-belief stream restore static-to-dynamic transfer? The decisive first result is a controlled failure curve plus oracle-contact rescue, not a broad two-hand benchmark replication. Unresolved: whether identical encoder/wrist states with distinct task-relevant contact modes can be generated robustly in Q\x27s released MuJoCo model; whether a history belief closes the oracle gap with only hardware-available encoders plus P\x27s external object tracking; and the engineering cost of bridging MuJoCo to DynaMAC/RLBench.
ready at #18

The wrist-plus-encoder baseline in #15 is diagnostic, not guaranteed to restore sufficiency. Q's underactuation means the same motor/cable position can be realized by different passive joint deflections under different contacts. The credible deployable extension is therefore a temporal belief \(b_t(c)=p(c_t\mid W_{0:t},E_{0:t},O_{0:t})\), potentially using tracked object motion; compare it with an oracle contact state. If encoders alone close the gap, that is an empirical simplification, not an assumption.

Best account: the pair supports a targeted falsification and extension of P, not the scan's generic hardware swap. P equates causal endogeneity with near-rigid low-variance wrist-object coupling and coordinates arms through opposite wrist pose. Q supplies a concrete class where contact causality is hybrid and partially observed: staged underactuated closure, compliant contacts, mutually coupled thumb channels, and encoder-only proprioception. Test whether success and link recall collapse as contact-mode aliasing increases, then restore them with a contact-belief-conditioned stream. This would turn a negative result into a generalization of dynamic task parameters from rigid \(SE(3)\) frames to hybrid contact beliefs.

Remaining unresolved: (i) whether P's released implementation includes gripper/contact signals omitted only 'for brevity'; (ii) whether Aero's MuJoCo assets include arm mounting and sufficiently validated contact compliance for bimanual tasks; (iii) how to define ground-truth causal contact influence beyond binary contact, especially during slip; and (iv) whether five static demonstrations cover enough contact modes to fit a belief model. These are implementation and experimental-design questions, not resolved by the papers.

Formal failure mode: let wrist pose be \(w_t\), object pose \(f_t\), and latent passive-joint/contact mode be \(z_t\). A compliant grasp can satisfy \(f_t=w_t h(z_t)\), so \(\operatorname{do}(w_t)\) changes \(f_t\) while \(H(f_t\mid w_t)>0\). Thus P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) identification of endogeneity with near-zero conditional spatial variance is not valid under the mechanics Q supplies. In-hand reorientation is the limiting counterexample: \(w_t\) stays fixed while \(f_t\) changes. Full derivation, experiment, and controls: ada/contact_latent_note.md.

Decisive experiment: in Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) tendon-level simulator, use a segmented handover or joint-carry task with controlled regrasp/microslip; train static demonstrations only; sweep spring/tendon stiffness, pad friction, geometry, and arm perturbation. Compare original wrist-pose DynaMAC, an oracle contact-causal link mask, current motor-conditioned streams, and a history-based belief over contact mode. Measure zero-shot success, link false negatives against simulator oracle, \(M_t^{(f)}\) versus compliance, and samples to fixed success. Rigid gripper and artificially rigid Aero controls isolate representation failure from integration/control.
ready at #24

Qualification to my #24 and note: compliance itself is not the treatment; repeatable compliant contact may still give low \(M_t^{(f)}\). The controlled variable should be contact-mode aliasing or relative-pose dispersion, created with spring stiffness, friction, object seating, and grasp type. Q explicitly models spring stiffness and randomizes fingertip/joint friction, but does not validate pad compliance or cable slack as sweep axes; those require new identification. The motor-conditioned arm is diagnostic because encoders need not resolve passive contact state.

A learned contact belief is not automatically compatible with P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) zero-shot claim: five static demonstrations may not contain the contact-mode transitions encountered after perturbation. The clean hierarchy is (A) original DynaMAC, (B) oracle interventional coupling/contact mode to establish that representation, not low-level control, causes the gap, then (C) a deployable temporal belief. If C needs dynamic training, it repairs robustness but does not preserve zero-shot static-to-dynamic generalization. Ground truth should be counterfactual influence of hand/wrist actions on object motion, not raw binary contact, which persists during non-supporting touch and slip.

Best account after cross-checking Emmy and Grace: the distinctive publication line is a failure boundary for DynaMAC\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) rigid-frame causal proxy under contact-mode aliasing, followed by an oracle and possibly belief-based rescue. Both partners independently found the same mechanism; Grace correctly narrows “compliance” to variable contact state, and Emmy proposes paired states with identical wrist/encoder observations but different required actions, which is the most decisive sufficiency test. This replaces the scan question rather than merely sharpening its hardware port.

Concluding after reading through #28. Unresolved: robust construction of paired aliased states in Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) released model; definition of an interventional influence oracle during slip; whether P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) code uses omitted gripper/contact signals; whether a belief trained only on static demonstrations can cover perturbation-induced contact modes; and MuJoCo/RLBench integration cost. These uncertainties bound feasibility but do not erase the targeted falsification.
ready at #28

Qualification to the proposed oracle in entries 12, 21, and 24: binary simulator contact is not ground-truth causal influence. Mere touching can be incidental, while sticking, rolling, slip, and multi-hand support distribute influence continuously. Define an interventional coupling score, for example \(I_{w\to f}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{\delta w}[d(f_{t+\Delta}^{\operatorname{do}(w+\delta w)},f_{t+\Delta})^2]/\mathbb{E}_{\delta w}[\|\delta w\|^2]\), under matched latent state and low-level commands, or use a simulator Jacobian/finite-difference analogue. Then test whether P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) statistic \(M_t^{(f)}\) classifies high \(I_{w\to f}\). Contact labels remain useful as the latent-mode target, but should not define causality.

A retained tracked-object stream or other task frames may compensate for an insufficient opposite-wrist frame, so aggregate task failure alone cannot identify the proposed mechanism. Use ablations with identical demonstrations and low-level controllers: original frame selection, forced wrist-only conditioning, forced object-stream retention, P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) mask with an oracle causal mask substituted, and a contact-belief stream. Detector error must precede and predict policy error; an oracle-mask rescue isolates frame selection from ordinary dexterous-control difficulty.

Revised best account after cross-checking Ada entries 23--24 and Grace entries 20--22: change the scan question from a broad Aero hardware replication to a test of P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) identification assumption. Q supplies a hybrid, partially observed mechanism in which \(f_t=w_t h(z_t)\): the wrist can causally move the object while latent passive-joint/contact mode \(z_t\) keeps \(H(f_t\mid w_t)>0\). P supplies the falsifiable equivalence between endogeneity and near-zero conditional spread, plus the opposite-wrist representation. The strongest publication is a controlled failure boundary between interventional coupling and \(M_t^{(f)}\), followed by oracle-mask rescue and, if possible, recovery with a temporal belief \(b_t(z)=p(z_t\mid W_{0:t},E_{0:t},O_{0:t},A_{0:t-1})\). This generalizes dynamic task parameters from rigid \(SE(3)\) frames to hybrid contact beliefs. Compliance alone is not the claim; variable contact mode or purposeful in-hand motion is required.

I will conclude on the targeted causal-identification study rather than the generic hardware port. Remaining unresolved: robust generation of aliased states in Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) released model; a defensible finite-horizon intervention score under feedback; whether P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) code uses gripper/contact information omitted from the paper; whether external object streams already eliminate the practical failure; and the MuJoCo--RLBench integration cost.
ready at #34

Refinement after checking P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) exact statistic: \(M_t^{(f)}\) is computed from the phase-indexed covariance of demonstrated end-effector poses expressed in frame \(f\), not directly from a trajectory-level estimate of \(H(f\mid w)\). The failure curve should therefore use within-phase dispersion of the relative transform \(w_t^{-1}f_t\), or paired phase-matched states, while holding segmentation and demonstrations fixed. Pooling across phases could manufacture variance unrelated to contact aliasing. P, lines 538--626, explicitly connects near-zero stream variance after rigid grasp to its link decision; Q, lines 230--244 and 282--364, supplies passive contact-dependent configurations hidden from the seven encoders.

Cross-check of Ada #27--28: the oracle-rescue experiment is the clean publishable core. A learned temporal belief is a stronger method contribution only if its information and training regime are stated precisely. If it is trained on dynamic contact transitions absent from the five static demonstrations, it no longer preserves P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) zero-shot static-to-dynamic claim. Report that as a robustness extension, or learn the belief from task-independent/system-identification data and separately test zero-shot task transfer. The decisive falsification remains phase-matched observation aliasing plus an oracle counterfactual-influence stream.
ready at #30
ready at #37

Update after Emmy \#31--32: raw contact labels are not a causal oracle, since touching may be incidental and influence during stick, roll, slip, or shared support is graded. Use a matched-state finite-difference intervention, for example \(I_{w\to f}(t)=\mathbb{E}_{\delta w}[d(f_{t+\Delta}^{\operatorname{do}(w+\delta w)},f_{t+\Delta})^2]/\mathbb{E}_{\delta w}[\lVert\delta w\rVert^2]\), with fixed horizon and feedback convention, and test whether P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) \(M_t^{(f)}\) detects high influence. The revised derivation and controls are in ada/contact_latent_note.md.

Aggregate task failure cannot isolate the proposed mechanism because P retains other tracked frames that may compensate for an insufficient opposite-wrist stream (P, observations and external vision reliance, lines 417 and 1091; its opposite-arm ablation explicitly forces reliance on the tracked object, line 1072). The decisive ablation set is original selection, forced wrist-only conditioning, forced object-stream retention, oracle causal-mask substitution, and contact-belief augmentation, holding demonstrations and controllers fixed. Detector error should precede policy error, and oracle-mask rescue must isolate selection from dexterous-control difficulty.

Grace \#36 identifies a necessary statistical refinement: P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) \(M_t^{(f)}\) comes from phase-indexed covariance of demonstrated end-effector poses in frame \(f\), not an unrestricted trajectory estimate of \(H(f\mid w)\). The failure boundary must compare phase-matched relative transforms \(w_t^{-1}f_t\) or paired states while holding segmentation and demonstrations fixed; pooling phases could create a spurious mismatch. I added this constraint to ada/contact_latent_note.md.

Final account after reading through \#41: replace the generic hardware port with a phase-matched causal-identification study. Establish divergence between P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) within-phase low-spread statistic \(M_t^{(f)}\) and a finite-horizon interventional wrist-to-object influence score under Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) latent contact modes; then require oracle-mask rescue under controlled stream ablations. A temporal contact belief is optional and preserves zero-shot task transfer only if learned without the held-out dynamic task transitions. Unresolved are aliased-state construction, intervention definition under feedback, compensation by external streams in ordinary tasks, omitted implementation signals, simulator fidelity, and interface cost.
ready at #43

ITERATE: The ledger supports a pair-specific, falsifiable hypothesis: under latent contact modes, high wrist-to-object causal influence can coexist with large within-phase relative-pose dispersion, defeating P's linkage proxy. Q8P8.tex traces this accurately but contains no constructed counterexample or oracle-mask rescue, so it is not yet a supported result. Action: Construct one phase-matched pair of simulator states with identical wrist poses and encoder readings but different task-relevant contact modes, then test whether high interventional influence coincides with failure of \(M_t^{(f)}\) and whether an oracle causal mask rescues the fixed policy.

In response to verifier #45, I constructed the missing phase-matched identifiability counterexample in grace/phase_matched_counterexample.md. Let \(s_A=(w_0,e_0,z_A,f_A)\) and \(s_B=(w_0,e_0,z_B,f_B)\) share wrist pose and seven encoder readings but differ in latent stable contact mode. With \(f=w h(z)\) and \(\delta f=J_z\delta w\), both modes may have nonzero causal wrist influence while \(h(z_A)\ne h(z_B)\), so phase-matched dispersion of \(w^{-1}f\) can make \(M_t^{(f)}\ge\tau_M\) despite high finite-horizon \(I_{w\to f}\). This is a paper-supported construction, not an empirical simulator result.

The empirical action requested by verifier #45 cannot be completed from the supplied workspace: it contains the papers and synthesis artifacts but no Aero simulator or DynaMAC implementation. The proposed stable aliased state pair remains an assumption requiring execution. The note specifies rejection criteria: inability to construct stable matched states, low interventional influence in the proposed coupled mode, or failure of an oracle mask to rescue a fixed policy. Therefore the publication claim must remain a concrete experiment proposal, not a supported result.
ready at #47

Response to verifier \#45 after inspecting the workspace: the only new executable is emmy/probe_aero_aliasing.py, which requires an external MuJoCo scene and only lists model state; no Aero scene/assets, bimanual task, demonstrations, DynaMAC policy, or fixed-policy masking interface is present. Thus an empirical state pair and oracle-mask rescue cannot be produced here. Grace \#46 supplies the correct paper-supported identifiability construction: phase-matched states can share \(w_0,e_0\) yet have \(z_A\ne z_B\), with high \(I_{w\to f}\) but \(M_t^{(f)}\ge\tau_M\). It remains a hypothesis until the released systems are integrated and run.

The verifier action asks for evidence beyond the supplied material. Q asserts release of a tendon-level MuJoCo model (Q, lines 200 and 333) and P asserts public code and benchmarks (P, line 329), but those releases are not included here. Downloading and integrating two external stacks, constructing arms/tasks/demonstrations, and implementing the oracle mask is a substantial new experiment, not a paper-reading cross-check. Do not relabel the analytic counterexample as a simulator result. Rejection criteria remain: no stable aliased pair, low measured interventional influence, or no fixed-policy oracle rescue.

Best account unchanged after reading through \#47: propose a phase-matched test of divergence between P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) within-phase linkage statistic and counterfactual wrist-to-object influence under Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) hidden contact modes, with oracle-mask rescue as the necessary empirical discriminator. The construction is supported; the positive result is not. Unresolved: external-stack integration, existence of robust matched states, intervention semantics under feedback, other-stream compensation, and whether static-only data can learn the contact belief.

ready at #51

Notation correction to grace/phase_matched_counterexample.md: all inline variables now use required TeX delimiters. Substantive status is unchanged. The construction gives phase-matched states \(s_A,s_B\) with matched \((w_0,e_0)\), distinct latent modes, and a possible divergence \(M_t^{(f)}\ge\tau_M\) while \(I_{w\to f}(t)>\tau_I\); it remains an analytic, paper-supported counterexample rather than an executed simulator result.
ready at #54

Responding to verifier #45, I cloned Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) released simulator from https://github.com/TetherIA/aero-hand-open and constructed an actual phase-matched proprioceptive alias in its \texttt{scene\_right.xml}. Restricting to states satisfying the PIP--DIP and thumb MCP--IP equality constraints, the seven-sensor Jacobian has rank \(7\) over an \(11\)-dimensional configuration parameterization, hence nullity \(4\). An exact scalar solve gives two states with the same fixed wrist and maximum encoder/tendon-sensor difference \(1.39\times10^{-17}\), but maximum fingertip-position difference \(9.02\,\mathrm{mm}\): the pinky changes from \((q_{\mathrm{MCP}},q_{\mathrm{PIP}}=q_{\mathrm{DIP}})=(0.45,0.53639096)\) to \((0.65,0.35774391)\) rad while its tendon length is held fixed. Code is in \texttt{emmy/probe\_aero\_aliasing.py}. This directly supports Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) claimed hidden mechanics and shows wrist plus encoders is not a sufficient hand-geometry state; it does not yet show different object support, high wrist-to-object intervention score, or failure of P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) mask.

The verifier\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) requested oracle-mask policy rescue cannot be executed from Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) released scene alone: the checked-out \texttt{scene\_right.xml} has \(16\) hand coordinates, a fixed wrist, seven actuators/sensors, and no object; P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) DynaMAC policy and its demonstration streams are a separate RLBench stack. The new 9.02 mm alias is a constructed necessary-condition counterexample to state sufficiency, not the requested causal or task-level result. Claiming publication readiness still requires adding an object/free wrist or arms, creating matched contact modes, computing phase-indexed \(M_t^{(f)}\), and showing oracle-mask rescue with a fixed policy.

Ada \#49--50 and Grace \#47 were correct about the initially supplied workspace but are now outdated in one respect: external network access allowed me to fetch and run Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) released MuJoCo model. This resolves existence of encoder-aliased hand geometries, not the stronger contact-causal or oracle-rescue questions. The distinction between the executed geometric witness in \#56 and Grace\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) analytic object-contact construction in \#46 must remain explicit.

Best account after reading through \#57: the broad hardware port should be replaced by a causal-identification study of P\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) rigid-frame linkage proxy. New executable evidence strengthens feasibility: Q\(\text{\textquotesingle}s\) actual model admits fixed-wrist, encoder-identical configurations separated by \(9.02\,\mathrm{mm}\) at a fingertip. This validates the hidden-state premise but not yet the publication claim. The decisive next experiment remains an object-bearing, phase-matched pair with high interventional wrist-to-object influence, failure of \(M_t^{(f)}\), and oracle-mask rescue. Unresolved: stable task-relevant contact modes, finite-horizon intervention under feedback, DynaMAC integration, external-stream compensation, and simulator-to-hardware fidelity.
